item.title: Diffusion & Flow Matching Part 8: Guided Generative Models
item.dc:creator: Hujie Wang
item.description:
NoteTL;DR
  • Guided generation conditions the model on additional information (e.g., text prompts, class labels)
  • CFG training: Standard loss + randomly drop conditioning with probability (10-20%)
  • CFG sampling: Amplify conditioning by extrapolating:
  • For Gaussian paths, CFG = amplifying the classifier gradient; for general flows it’s purely empirical

So far, the generative models we have discussed are all unconditional models, i.e., they generate samples from the target probability distribution without any additional information. In this post, we will discuss how to make these models conditional on some additional information like a text prompt .

To avoid notation and terminology clash with the use of the word “conditional” to refer to conditioning on , we will use the term “guided” to refer specifically to conditioning on .

Def: Guided Generative Model

A guided diffusion model is defined by the SDE:

When , the SDE reduces to the ODE for guided flow matching:

Guidance for Flow Models

Now let us imagine we have a label for each data . For images, some of them are “dog” and some of them are “cat”. Given a fixed label , we can think of as a “slice” of the data distribution — the subset of data points with that label.

Given a fixed label , the CFM loss is defined as before:

The target is exactly the same as in unconditional flow matching (see Part 3): the vector field that transports noise toward data point . For Gaussian paths with :

How does training on give us ? This is the marginalization trick again. The key insight is:

Why? Because the probability path only depends on — once you know the specific data point , the label provides no additional information about how to add noise to it. The noise-adding process is purely mechanical and doesn’t care about labels.

Therefore, the marginalization formula from Part 4 applies directly:

What does this mean? Given noisy sample and label , the marginal vector field is an average over all possible clean data points that could have generated , weighted by the posterior . The label constrains which values are plausible, but once a specific is chosen, the vector field is the same regardless of .

We never compute this expectation explicitly — least-squares regression does it for us (see Part 6). By sampling and regressing against , the model learns .

You can think of as a specific model just for the data slice with label . We could build separate models for each label and train them separately, but this is not efficient. Instead, we want to train a single model that works for all , so the model takes input instead of only as before.

Now, we want to minimize the expected loss over all possible labels . The total loss is the expectation of the label-specific losses :

By the definition of joint probability:

we can merge these two expectations into one:

Substituting back, we get:

In practice, sampling would involve a dataloader that returns batches of both and .

The Problem: Weak Conditioning

While the above training procedure is theoretically valid, it was empirically observed that images generated with this procedure did not fit well enough to the desired label . The generated samples were correct on average, but lacked the strong conditioning that users wanted.

TipThe Solution: Amplify Conditioning at Sampling Time

Both Classifier Guidance and Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) are sampling-time techniques. The idea is the same: scale up the “conditioning direction” to get stronger adherence to the label .

The derivations below show why this works mathematically. The difference between the two methods is how you compute the conditioning direction:

Method How to get the conditioning direction Extra training required?
Classifier Guidance Train a separate classifier Yes (classifier)
CFG Use label dropout so one model estimates both terms No

Classifier Guidance

ImportantImportant: Gaussian Paths Required

The derivation below relies on Gaussian probability paths . The score is a property of the marginal distribution — it exists mathematically regardless of whether we’re training a diffusion model or flow model. For Gaussian paths, the conversion formula relates this score to the vector field, enabling the derivation below.

Recall from Part 7 that for Gaussian conditional probability path , we can use the conversion formula to write the marginal vector field in terms of the marginal score:

Replacing the vector field and score function with guided ones, we get:

we can expand the guided score function using Bayes’ rule:

Plugging back to the guided vector field, we get:

Notice the shape of the above equation: the guided vector field is a sum of the unguided vector field plus a guided score . The term is considered as a classifier which gives the likelihood of the label given the data .

It has been empirically observed that scaling up the contribution of by a guidance scale gives better outputs.

Note that this is a heuristic: for , we do not sample from the true guided distribution .

In the early works, people trained actual classifiers and use them to guide via the above procedure. But it has drawbacks:

  • Requires training an extra classifier on noisy data
  • The classifier must handle all noise levels
  • Complicates the training pipeline

Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG)

Classifier-free guidance (CFG) achieves the same amplification without training a separate classifier. The key idea: rewrite the classifier gradient in terms of vector fields we can learn from a single model.

Deriving the CFG Formula

Using Bayes’ rule, we can rewrite the classifier gradient:

Plugging back into the scaled guided vector field :

From the conversion formula, we can express scores in terms of vector fields:

Substituting back and simplifying (the and terms cancel):

This is the CFG formula: the scaled guided vector field is a linear combination of the unguided and guided vector fields. When , we extrapolate beyond the conditional direction, amplifying the effect of conditioning.

Training

To use the CFG formula, we need both (guided) and (unguided). Instead of training two separate models, we train a single model that handles both by introducing a null token :

Training procedure:

  1. Sample — a data point with its label
  2. With probability (typically 10-20%), replace with
  3. Minimize the CFM loss:

Why does this work? The target is always the same — it doesn’t depend on . What changes is the model input:

  • When we keep : the model learns conditional vector field
  • When we drop : the model learns marginal vector field

By training with on random samples from all classes, the model learns the marginal (average over all conditionals) — exactly what we need for the CFG formula.

NoteKey Point

The training loss is identical to standard guided CFM. The only change is randomly dropping the label with probability . The CFG formula is not used during training — it only appears at sampling time.

Sampling

At inference time, we use the trained model to compute both outputs and combine them:

Equivalently:

Sampling procedure:

  1. Sample (e.g., Gaussian noise)
  2. At each step, run the model twice: once with , once with
  3. Combine outputs using the CFG formula with guidance scale
  4. Integrate the ODE/SDE using

The guidance scale controls the strength of conditioning:

  • : No amplification (standard conditional generation)
  • : Amplified conditioning (sharper, more “on-prompt” samples)
  • : Over-saturation (artifacts, reduced diversity)
WarningWhat about non-Gaussian flows?

The CFG formula is just a weighted interpolation — you can apply it to any vector fields regardless of path type. What changes is the interpretation:

  • Gaussian paths: This interpolation = amplifying a classifier gradient (the derivation above)
  • Non-Gaussian paths: The formula still works empirically, but we lose the classifier gradient interpretation. Why does interpolating vector fields improve conditioning? It remains theoretically unclear.

In practice, most modern systems (Stable Diffusion, Flux, etc.) use Gaussian paths, so this distinction rarely matters.

Guidance for Flow Models

NoteSummary

We extended flow matching and diffusion models to guided generation — conditioning on labels, text prompts, or other side information .

Classifier-free guidance (CFG) in two steps:

Phase What happens Formula used
Training Random label dropout with probability Standard CFM loss
Sampling Combine conditional + unconditional outputs

The derivation shows why CFG works: for Gaussian paths, the difference approximates the classifier gradient . Scaling by amplifies this gradient, improving sample quality at the cost of diversity.

References

[1] Classifier-Free Guidance is a Predictor-Corrector. Bradley & Nakkiran. arXiv 2024.

[2] Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance. Ho & Salimans. NeurIPS Workshop 2021.

[3] Diffusion Models Beat GANs on Image Synthesis. Dhariwal & Nichol. NeurIPS 2021.

[4] Guided Flows for Generative Modeling and Decision Making. Zheng et al. arXiv 2023.

TipExample: Denoising Diffusion Models: Score Matching

As a remark, the term “denoising diffusion models” are simply diffusion models with Gaussian probability path .

As before, the conditional score is

The problem: The weighting blows up as (near for schedules like ), causing numerical instability.

The DDPM approach (Ho et al., 2020) makes two independent modifications:

1. Reparameterize to noise prediction. The loss is zero when , i.e., when . This motivates defining a noise prediction network:

With this reparameterization, the CSM loss becomes:

Note: the weighting is still there! Reparameterization only changes what the network outputs (score → noise), not the weighting.

2. Drop the weighting (empirical choice). Ho et al. found that simply removing works better in practice:

Why does dropping the weighting work? Both losses share the same global minimum (zero when for all ). What differs is the optimization landscape:

  • Weighted loss: Heavily penalizes errors at small (nearly clean images) → unstable gradients, network focuses on easy samples

This is an empirical finding, not a mathematical consequence. The simple loss happens to produce better sample quality.

Note on time conditioning: The network takes both the noisy image and time as input. It needs to know the signal-to-noise ratio: the same creates different amounts of visible corruption at different times. item.title: Diffusion & Flow Matching Part 6: Conditional and Marginal Score Functions
item.dc:creator: Hujie Wang
item.description:
NoteTL;DR
  • The score function tells us which direction increases probability — it’s the key to extending flow matching to SDEs
  • We can’t compute the marginal score directly, but we can express it as an expectation of conditional scores (which we can compute analytically)
  • The magic of training: least-squares regression automatically computes the right expectation — no intractable integrals required!
  • Real-world impact: This is how Stable Diffusion, DALL-E, and Sora learn to denoise images

In the previous post, we constructed the training target for flow matching models. Now we face a new challenge: how do we extend this to SDEs?

The answer involves a beautiful mathematical object called the score function — the gradient of log probability. This post shows how score functions connect ODEs to SDEs, and reveals the elegant trick that makes training tractable.

Let’s start with the key theorem that bridges these two worlds.

TipTheorem: SDE Extension Trick

Let be the flow matching vector field that generates the probability path via the ODE (i.e., the ODE with satisfies ).

For any diffusion coefficient , we can construct an SDE that follows the same probability path :

where is the marginal score function of .

The same identity holds if we replace the marginal probability and vector field with the conditional probability and vector field .

From Marginal to Conditional Scores

The theorem above requires the marginal score . But there’s a problem: computing this directly requires integrating over all possible data points — computationally intractable!

The solution is to express the marginal score as an expectation of conditional scores , which we can compute analytically.

Step-by-step reasoning:

  3. Leibniz rule: swap and

Swapping and requires regularity conditions (the Leibniz integral rule). This holds when the integrand is smooth and its derivative is bounded by an integrable function — standard assumptions for “nice” probability densities.

NoteDerivation of the last step

The key is to rewrite using the chain rule for logarithms.

(This is the multivariate generalization of from single-variable calculus.)

Rearranging:

Substituting this into the integral:

Since doesn’t depend on , we can move it inside the integral:

Notice that by Bayes’ theorem (since ), so this is an expectation over the posterior:

The conditional score function is usually something we can calculate analytically (e.g., for Gaussian conditionals).

NoteExample: Gaussian Conditional Score Function

For a Gaussian conditional where , the conditional score function is:

Derivation: The multivariate Gaussian PDF with mean and covariance is:

For isotropic covariance (a diagonal matrix with on every diagonal):

  • Determinant: (product of diagonal entries), so
  • Inverse: , so

Substituting into the Gaussian PDF:

Taking the log:

Taking the gradient with respect to (the constant term vanishes):

(We used , which follows from .)

Proving the SDE Extension Trick

Now that we understand conditional scores, let’s prove why the SDE Extension Trick works. The key tool is the Fokker-Planck equation, which extends the continuity equation (from Part 4) to handle SDEs.

TipTheorem: Fokker-Planck Equation

Consider an SDE:

Then for all iff the Fokker-Planck equation holds:

where is the Laplacian operator

We know that is a valid vector field that follows the probability path for the ODE, then it must satisfy the continuity equation:

NoteWhy can we start with the continuity equation?

This may seem circular: we’re proving something about SDEs, but we start with the continuity equation (which is for ODEs). Here’s why this works:

  1. We already have a probability path and vector field from flow matching
  2. By construction, was defined so that the ODE follows
  3. Therefore, the continuity equation above holds — this is just restating what we already know

The question is: given this , can we find an SDE drift that also follows ? We substitute the continuity equation (a known fact) into the Fokker-Planck equation and solve for what the SDE drift must be.

Our goal is to find an SDE drift term that satisfies the Fokker-Planck equation.

It turns out we can algebraically derive the SDE drift term from the continuity equation:

Note that we already have the last term in the Fokker-Planck equation, now we just need to manipulate the first two terms to match the Fokker-Planck equation.

Therefore, if we set

then it satisfies the Fokker-Planck equation.

To understand this intuitively, the SDE can be seen as follows:

Intuition: The Drunken Marching Band

Imagine a marching band trying to move from one end of a football field to the other in perfect formation.

The ODE (The Sober Band)

  • Every band member walks in a straight, precalculated line ()
  • From the sky, the ‘A’ shape moves smoothly across the field ()

The SDE (The Drunken Band)

Now imagine we force every band member to be drunk. They stumble randomly ().

The problem: If they try to walk the same path as the sober band plus the stumbling, they will wander off. The ‘A’ shape will get fuzzy and eventually dissolve into a blob. The “probability path” is ruined.

The “Forcing” (The Drift Correction)

To fix this, we have to cheat. We have to “force” the SDE to match the ODE’s shape.

  • The solution: We tell band members: “Since you are drunk and stumbling outward, you must strictly aim slightly inward to compensate”.

If the stumbling pushes them away from the formation, we add an extra “Pull” (correction drift) pointing back towards the center of the formation.

  • The result: individual band members are stumbling like crazy (stochastic), but because we added the extra “inward pull”, the macro shape (helicopter view, i.e., the probability distribution) looks identical to the sober band.
NoteSummary

We proved the SDE extension trick: given an ODE with drift , we can add arbitrary noise while preserving the same probability path by correcting the drift:

The correction term points toward high-probability regions, counteracting the dispersion from noise (the “drunken marching band” needs to aim inward to maintain formation).

For training, we showed that the marginal score equals an expectation of conditional scores:

The magic: least-squares regression computes this expectation automatically — we never need to evaluate the intractable posterior explicitly.

How Training Actually Works

You might wonder: “I know how to compute for a given , but what about the other terms? How do I compute the expectation over ?”

The key insight is that we don’t compute the integral explicitly. Instead, we use a clever sampling trick.

ImportantThe Training Trick: Reverse the Sampling Order

The expectation is over the posterior , which is hard to sample from. But we can reverse the sampling order:

  1. Sample — pick a data point
  2. Sample — generate its noisy version at time
  3. Compute — this we know analytically!
  4. Train to predict this value

Why this works: When we sample this way, we’re sampling from the joint distribution .

The training loss becomes:

NoteWhy does this give us the marginal score?

This is the score matching identity. When we minimize the loss above, the optimal satisfies:

Intuitively: for a given , different ’s could have produced it. The network learns to average over all possible ’s, weighted by how likely each was to produce this — which is exactly the posterior .

But wait — where did the normalization go?

Recall from earlier that the marginal score involves . The denominator is intractable (it’s a marginal over all possible ’s). So how can training work without computing it?

The answer lies in a fundamental property of least-squares regression:

When you minimize squared error over samples from a joint distribution , the optimal predictor equals the conditional expectation .

Mathematically, if we minimize:

then the optimal solution is .

Applied to our training:

  • We sample from the joint
  • We regress onto
  • The optimal automatically becomes

The posterior weighting emerges implicitly from the sampling frequencies: data points that are more likely to produce a given will appear more often in our training batches at that . The neural network learns this weighting through gradient descent — we never need to compute explicitly!

In practice, you never compute — you just sample and regress! The neural network implicitly learns to marginalize over .

What’s Next

We’ve established the theoretical foundation: we know what to train (the score function) and why the training procedure works (least-squares regression gives us the conditional expectation).

In the next two posts, we’ll dive into the practical details:

  • Part 7: The complete training algorithm — how to implement score matching in practice
  • Part 8: Sampling and inference — how to generate new samples from the trained model

item.title: Diffusion & Flow Matching Part 5: Diffusion Models and SDEs
item.dc:creator: Hujie Wang
item.description:
NoteTL;DR
  • Diffusion models add stochasticity to the ODE:
  • Key insight: We derive SDEs by thinking in terms of infinitesimal updates rather than derivatives
  • The Brownian motion term represents continuous random perturbations
  • Setting recovers the deterministic ODE from flow matching

Diffusion Models: Adding Stochasticity

In Parts 2-4, we developed flow matching — a framework where a neural network learns a vector field that transports noise to data via an ODE:

This is elegant, but there’s another approach that dominated generative modeling before flow matching emerged: diffusion models. Instead of following a deterministic path, diffusion models add randomness at each step.

Why would we want randomness? It turns out that stochasticity can help exploration during sampling, improve sample diversity, and connects to a rich mathematical theory. Let’s see how.

The Problem with Derivatives

Before we add stochasticity, let’s revisit how we think about ODEs. The standard formulation uses derivatives:

This says: “the instantaneous rate of change of equals the vector field evaluated at .”

WarningThe Challenge

Derivatives are elegant for deterministic systems, but they become problematic when we want to add randomness. A random process doesn’t have a well-defined derivative in the classical sense — the path is too “jagged” due to the random perturbations.

To add stochasticity properly, we need a different way to think about dynamics — one that doesn’t rely on taking derivatives.

From Derivatives to Infinitesimal Updates

Instead of asking “what is the derivative?”, we can ask: “what happens over a small time step ?”

Starting from the ODE, we can write:

where is an error term that goes to zero as .

NoteWhere does the error term come from?

The error term comes from the definition of the derivative itself. The derivative is defined as a limit:

When is small but not zero, the finite difference is only an approximation to the true derivative:

Since the ODE says , we get the equation above. The key property is that as , which is exactly what the limit definition guarantees.

What about SDEs? When we add stochasticity, becomes a random variable, which means the error is also random. We can no longer simply say “” — we need to specify in what sense a random quantity vanishes.

The rigorous statement uses mean square convergence:

This says the typical size of the error (measured by root-mean-square) goes to zero. Think of it as: “on average, the error becomes negligible.”

Rearranging:

TipIntuition

This says: “where you end up = where you started + (small step) × (direction) + (small error)”. As , the error term vanishes and we recover the ODE behavior.

This infinitesimal update formulation is exactly what we need. It describes the dynamics without ever taking a derivative — we just describe how the state changes over small time intervals.

Adding Stochasticity: The SDE

Now we can add randomness naturally. At each small time step, we add a random perturbation:

Here:

  • is the drift — the deterministic direction (same as in flow matching)
  • is the diffusion coefficient — controls how much randomness we add
  • is Brownian motion — a mathematical model of continuous random motion
  • is the random increment over the time interval

As , we write this compactly as the stochastic differential equation (SDE):

ImportantKey Point

Notice that we never took a derivative of the random process! The SDE notation is shorthand for the infinitesimal update, not an actual derivative. This is why SDEs can describe processes with random, non-differentiable paths.

When , the SDE reduces to an ODE, and we recover flow matching.

NoteDefinition: Diffusion Model

A diffusion model is defined by:

The drift is parameterized by a neural network, and is typically a simple distribution like . Compare this to flow matching, which has the same structure but with (no stochasticity).

WarningNo Flow Map for SDEs

Recall that for ODEs, we had a flow map that deterministically mapped initial points to their positions at time . SDEs don’t have this! Given a starting point , the value is no longer fully determined — the stochastic evolution means different runs produce different trajectories. This is a fundamental difference that will affect how we think about probability distributions.

What is Brownian Motion?

Brownian motion (also called a Wiener process) is the mathematical model of “pure randomness” evolving continuously in time.

TipIntuition: From Random Walk to Brownian Motion

Start with something familiar: a random walk. At each step, flip a coin and move +1 or -1. After steps, your position is the sum of random ’s.

Now speed this up: take smaller steps more frequently. If you take steps of size per unit time, something magical happens as — you get Brownian motion. The scaling is crucial: it ensures the variance grows linearly with time (not too fast, not too slow).

The result is a continuous path that:

  • Never stops jiggling (infinitely many tiny steps)
  • Has no preferred direction (mean 0)
  • Accumulates uncertainty over time (variance = time elapsed)

Formally, Brownian motion has these properties:

  • Starts at zero:
  • Independent increments: is independent of everything up to time
  • Gaussian increments:
  • Continuous paths: is continuous in (but nowhere differentiable!)

Using these properties, we can simulate an SDE over a small time step. Starting from the SDE:

Over a finite step of size :

  • becomes the step size
  • becomes the increment

By the Gaussian increments property, . We can sample from this distribution using the reparameterization trick:

This works because scaling a sample by gives variance (since ).

Putting it together, we get the Euler-Maruyama discretization:

This is the simplest way to simulate an SDE numerically. Notice how the noise scales with , not — this is a fundamental property of Brownian motion.

The Diffusion Coefficient

The diffusion coefficient controls the “temperature” of the random noise:

  • Large : More exploration, paths spread out quickly
  • Small : More deterministic, paths stay close to the drift
  • : Pure ODE (flow matching)

In diffusion models, is typically a schedule that varies with time. Common choices:

Schedule Used in
Variance Preserving (VP) DDPM
Variance Exploding (VE) NCSN/NCSNv2
Sub-VP Interpolation Score SDE

The choice of schedule affects sample quality, training stability, and generation speed.

Forward and Reverse Processes

In diffusion models, we typically define:

  1. Forward process: An SDE that gradually adds noise to data until it becomes pure noise
  2. Reverse process: An SDE that removes noise, going from noise back to data

The forward process is usually simple and fixed (e.g., just adding Gaussian noise). The challenge is learning to reverse it.

NoteThe Key Question

Given the forward SDE that corrupts data into noise, what is the reverse SDE that transforms noise back into data?

It turns out there’s a beautiful mathematical result: the reverse SDE depends on something called the score function — the gradient of the log probability density. But how do we learn this score function? That’s the subject of the next post.

NoteSummary

We extended flow matching to SDEs by thinking in terms of infinitesimal updates rather than derivatives:

The Brownian motion term models continuous randomness — Gaussian increments with variance proportional to time elapsed. Setting recovers the deterministic ODE.

ODE (Flow Matching) SDE (Diffusion)
Deterministic paths Stochastic paths
One trajectory per Distribution of trajectories

The open question: how do we train a network to reverse the SDE? The answer involves the score function.

What’s Next?

We’ve seen how to add stochasticity to get an SDE, but we haven’t yet addressed the core challenge: how do we train a neural network to reverse the diffusion process?

In Part 6, we’ll discover:

  • The score function and why it’s central to diffusion models
  • Denoising score matching — the clever trick that makes training tractable
  • The probability flow ODE — how every SDE has an equivalent deterministic formulation
  • How this connects diffusion models back to flow matching

item.title: Diffusion & Flow Matching Part 4: The Flow Matching Loss
item.dc:creator: Hujie Wang
item.description:
NoteTL;DR
  • The problem: We have conditional vector fields , but at generation time we don’t know
  • The solution: The marginalization trick — training on conditional targets is equivalent to learning the marginal vector field

The Flow Matching Loss: Why Training Works

In the previous post, we constructed conditional probability paths and conditional vector fields. But there’s a fundamental problem: these are conditional on knowing the target data point . At generation time, we don’t know — that’s what we’re trying to generate!

This post explains how the marginalization trick solves this problem.

The Problem We’re Solving

Let’s step back and understand what we’re trying to achieve.

NoteOur Goal

Train a neural network that can transform noise into samples from . To do this, we need a training target — a vector field that the network should learn to approximate.

The ideal target is the marginal vector field that follows the marginal probability path . If our network learns this, it can generate samples by:

  1. Start with noise
  2. Follow the learned vector field:
  3. Arrive at a sample from at

The problem: We can’t compute directly! It would require integrating over the entire data distribution — intractable.

The solution: The marginalization trick. It tells us that:

  1. We can design simple conditional vector fields (one for each data point )
  2. Training on these conditional targets is equivalent to training on the marginal target
  3. The trained network will learn the marginal vector field — exactly what we need for generation

This is why the marginalization trick is so powerful: it turns an intractable problem into a tractable one.

The Marginalization Trick

Given a conditional vector field that follows the conditional probability path , we can construct a marginal vector field that follows the marginal probability path :

This is the marginalization trick. To prove it, we will use the continuity equation.

The Continuity Equation

TipTheorem: Continuity Equation

We will skip the proof of the continuity equation.

If the divergence is negative, it means that the vector field is pointing inwards towards this point.

The divergence measures the net outflow of density from a point. And the negative divergence means the net inflow of density into this point.

If you are not familiar with this or vector calculus, I recommend you watch the The Divergence of a Vector Field: Sources and Sinks by Steve Brunton. He also talks about the continuity equation in the context of fluid dynamics here: The Continuity Equation: A PDE for Mass Conservation, from Gauss’s Divergence Theorem.

Physics Background

Let me briefly explain the continuity equation, it originates from physics:

where is the mass density and is the mass flux. The equation was derived from Gauss’s Divergence Theorem, it’s also called mass conservation equation.

The flux is defined as the product of mass density and the the velocity field :

Intuitively, the flux measures the amount of mass flow rate per unit area through a surface.

The mass conservation equation states that the rate of change of mass in a volume is equal to the net outflow of mass through the surface of the volume. It’s a fundamental law that mass cannot be created or destroyed within a defined system.

In the context of flow models, the mass density is the probability density and the velocity field is the vector field . The continuity equation then becomes:

This is the continuity equation in the context of flow models.

Proof of the Marginalization Trick

Now we can return to the marginalization trick, we just need to show that the marginal vector field satisfies the continuity equation.

By the Continuity Equation, we have shown that the marginal vector field satisfies the continuity equation. Therefore, the marginal vector field follows the marginal probability path and we are done.

TipKey Takeaway

The marginalization trick is what makes flow matching tractable. Here’s the practical workflow:

  1. Design a simple conditional vector field (e.g., pointing from noise toward data point )
  2. Train by sampling pairs and minimizing
  3. Generate by following the learned from noise — it approximates the marginal vector field

The magic: even though we only ever see conditional targets during training, the network learns the marginal vector field that generates the full data distribution.

NoteSummary

We proved the marginalization trick: training on conditional targets is mathematically equivalent to training on the intractable marginal . The key step was showing that the cross-term simplifies when we expand the marginal definition — the intractable cancels.

This gives us the Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) loss:

The flow matching framework is now complete for deterministic sampling. Next, we’ll add stochasticity to get diffusion models.

What’s Next?

We’ve now covered the complete flow matching framework — from vector fields to probability paths to the training loss. But remember from Part 1 that diffusion models take a different approach: they add stochasticity to the process.

In the next post, we’ll see how diffusion models generalize flow matching by adding a noise term to the ODE, turning it into an SDE. We’ll discover:

  • How to derive SDEs using infinitesimal updates instead of derivatives
  • Why the random term enables new behaviors
  • The connection between Brownian motion and continuous randomness

item.title: Diffusion & Flow Matching Part 2: Understanding Flows
item.dc:creator: Hujie Wang
item.description:
NoteTL;DR
  • A vector field tells you which direction to move at each point in space
  • A flow is the map that shows where every point ends up after following the vector field
  • This is the mathematical foundation for flow matching: we’ll learn a vector field that “flows” noise into data

Understanding Flows

In flow matching, we learn a vector field that transports samples from noise to data. But what exactly is a vector field? And what does it mean to “follow” one? This post builds the intuition you’ll need for everything that follows.

Intuition: Think of a River

Imagine a river with currents flowing in different directions at different locations.

  • Vector field : The current at each point — it tells a particle “if you’re here, move in this direction”
  • Trajectory : Following one leaf dropped in the river — where is that specific leaf at time ?
  • Flow : A map that answers “where does any leaf end up at time , given it started at position ?”

The key insight: tracks one particle, while describes how the entire space transforms over time.

Formal Definition

Every ODE is defined by a vector field . A solution starting from must satisfy:

In words: “your velocity equals whatever the vector field says at your current location.”

From Trajectory to Flow

The trajectory answers: “where am I at time , given I started at ?”

But what if we want to know the answer for any starting point? That’s the flow : a function that takes any starting position and returns where it ends up at time .

For one specific starting point , the trajectory and flow give the same answer. But the flow is more general — it’s the entire “transformation rule” for all points.

NoteSummary

We established the core vocabulary: a vector field assigns directions to points in space, a trajectory follows those directions from a single starting point, and a flow describes where all points end up. The relationship: .

Concept Notation What it answers
Vector field “What direction should I move at position ?”
Trajectory “Where is this one particle at time ?”
Flow “Where does any point end up at time ?”

This is the foundation for everything that follows. In the next post, we’ll use flows to transform probability distributions — the key to generative modeling.

What’s Next?

We now understand how vector fields generate flows. But for generative modeling, we need flows that transform probability distributions — specifically, from noise to data.

In the next post, we’ll see how to construct probability paths that smoothly interpolate between a noise distribution and the data distribution, and the vector fields that generate them.

item.title: Diffusion & Flow Matching Part 1: Introduction
item.dc:creator: Timothy Wang
item.description:
NoteTL;DR
  • Diffusion models gradually add noise to data, then learn to reverse the process
  • Flow matching learns a velocity field that directly transports noise to data
  • Both achieve state-of-the-art results; flow matching is often simpler to train

Series Overview

This multi-part series explores the theory behind modern generative models. Each post builds on the previous one:

Part Topic What You’ll Learn
Part 1 Introduction (this post) High-level overview of diffusion and flow matching
Part 2 Understanding Flows Vector fields, trajectories, and flows — the foundation
Part 3 Probability Paths How we define paths from noise to data
Part 4 The Flow Matching Loss The marginalization trick that makes training work
Part 5 Diffusion Models & SDEs Stochastic differential equations and Brownian motion
Part 6 Score Functions Conditional and marginal scores, the training trick
Part 7 Training Algorithms CFM, DDPM, and the conversion formulas

What Are We Building?

Diffusion models and flow matching power today’s best generative AI systems — Stable Diffusion, DALL-E, Midjourney, and Flux. Despite their different formulations, both solve the same fundamental problem:

How do we learn to transform random noise into structured data?

If we can do this, we can generate new images, audio, video, or any data type by starting with random noise and “flowing” toward realistic samples.

Diffusion Models: The Noisy Path

The key idea behind diffusion models is surprisingly simple:

  1. Forward process: Take real data and gradually corrupt it with noise until it becomes pure random noise
  2. Reverse process: Train a neural network to undo this corruption step by step

Think of it like this: if you slowly blur a photograph until it’s unrecognizable static, the neural network learns to “unblur” it. At generation time, you start with pure static and apply the learned unblurring process to create a new image.

The forward process is fixed (just adding noise), so the only thing we need to learn is how to reverse it. The network is trained to predict how much noise was added at each step.

Flow Matching: The Direct Path

Flow matching takes a more direct approach:

  1. Define a path: Specify how to smoothly interpolate between noise and data
  2. Learn the velocity: Train a neural network to predict the direction of motion along this path

Imagine dropping a leaf into a river. The current (vector field) tells the leaf which way to move at each moment. If we design the currents correctly, leaves dropped anywhere in the “noise region” will flow toward the “data region.”

The simplest path is a straight line between a noise sample and a data sample. The network learns the velocity field that produces these straight-line trajectories.

How Do They Compare?

Aspect Diffusion Flow Matching
Corruption process Gradual noise addition Direct interpolation
What the network learns How much noise to remove Which direction to move
Sampling method Iterative denoising Following the learned flow
Underlying theory Score matching Optimal transport
Path type Stochastic (random) Deterministic (fixed)

The Deep Connection

Despite their different presentations, diffusion and flow matching are deeply related. Every diffusion model has an equivalent “probability flow” formulation that looks like flow matching. The score function (gradient of log probability) in diffusion corresponds to the velocity field in flow matching.

This connection means insights from one framework often transfer to the other, and modern systems sometimes combine ideas from both.

NoteSummary

We’ve seen two paradigms for generative modeling: diffusion (add noise, learn to denoise) and flow matching (learn a velocity field that transports noise to data). Despite their different motivations, they share deep mathematical structure — every diffusion model has an equivalent ODE formulation.

This series will make these connections precise. We’ll build up the theory piece by piece: first understanding what flows are (Part 2), then constructing probability paths (Part 3), deriving training losses (Part 4), adding stochasticity (Part 5), and finally connecting everything through score functions (Parts 6-7).

What’s Next?

In the following posts, we’ll develop the mathematical machinery to understand these methods properly:

  • Part 2: We’ll define what “flows” and “vector fields” actually mean
  • Part 3: We’ll see how to construct paths from noise to data
  • Part 4: We’ll discover the clever trick that makes training tractable
  • Part 5: We’ll add stochasticity to get SDEs and understand Brownian motion
  • Part 6: We’ll learn about score functions and the training trick

By the end, you’ll understand not just what these models do, but why they work.
